source: We had lain thus in bed, chatting and napping at short intervals, and Queequeg now and then affectionately throwing his brown tattooed legs over mine, and then drawing them back; so entirely sociable and free and easy were we; when, at last, by reason of our confabulations, what little nappishness remained in us altogether departed, and we felt like getting up again, though day-break was yet some way down the future.

Yes, we became very wakeful; so much so that our recumbent position began to grow wearisome, and by little and little we found ourselves sitting up; the clothes well tucked around us, leaning against the head-board with our four knees drawn up close together, and our two noses bending over them, as if our kneepans were warming-pans. We felt very nice and snug, the more so since it was so chilly out of doors; indeed out of bed-clothes too, seeing that there was no fire in the room. The more so, I say, because truly to enjoy bodily warmth, some small part of you must be cold, for there is no quality in this world that is not what it is merely by contrast. Nothing exists in itself. If you flatter yourself that you are all over comfortable, and have been so a long time, then you cannot be said to be comfortable any more. But if, like Queequeg and me in the bed, the tip of your nose or the crown of your head be slightly chilled, why then, indeed, in the general consciousness you feel most delightfully and unmistakably warm. For this reason a sleeping apartment should never be furnished with a fire, which is one of the luxurious discomforts of the rich. For the height of this sort of deliciousness is to have nothing but the blanket between you and your snugness and the cold of the outer air. Then there you lie like the one warm spark in the heart of an arctic crystal.

We had been sitting in this crouching manner for some time, when all at once I thought I would open my eyes; for when between sheets, whether by day or by night, and whether asleep or awake, I have a way of always keeping my eyes shut, in order the more to concentrate the snugness of being in bed. Because no man can ever feel his own identity aright except his eyes be closed; as if darkness were indeed the proper element of our essences, though light be more congenial to our clayey part. Upon opening my eyes then, and coming out of my own pleasant and self-created darkness into the imposed and coarse outer gloom of the unilluminated twelve-o’clock-at-night, I experienced a disagreeable revulsion. Nor did I at all object to the hint from Queequeg that perhaps it were best to strike a light, seeing that we were so wide awake; and besides he felt a strong desire to have a few quiet puffs from his Tomahawk. Be it said, that though I had felt such a strong repugnance to his smoking in the bed the night before, yet see how elastic our stiff prejudices grow when love once comes to bend them. For now I liked nothing better than to have Queequeg smoking by me, even in bed, because he seemed to be full of such serene household joy then. I no more felt unduly concerned for the landlord’s policy of insurance. I was only alive to the condensed confidential comfortableness of sharing a pipe and a blanket with a real friend. With our shaggy jackets drawn about our shoulders, we now passed the Tomahawk from one to the other, till slowly there grew over us a blue hanging tester of smoke, illuminated by the flame of the new-lit lamp.

Whether it was that this undulating tester rolled the savage away to far distant scenes, I know not, but he now spoke of his native island; and, eager to hear his history, I begged him to go on and tell it. He gladly complied. Though at the time I but ill comprehended not a few of his words, yet subsequent disclosures, when I had become more familiar with his broken phraseology, now enable me to present the whole story such as it may prove in the mere skeleton I give.

modern_en.title: Chapter 11 — Nightgown
paragraphs: We had lain in bed chatting and napping in short intervals, with Queequeg now and then affectionately throwing his brown tattooed legs over mine and drawing them back. We were so entirely sociable and free and easy together. At last, our confabulations chased away what little nappishness remained in us, and we felt like getting up — though dawn was still some way off.

We grew so wide awake that lying down became tiresome. Little by little we sat up, bedclothes tucked snugly around us, leaning against the headboard with our four knees drawn up close together and our two noses bent over them, as if our kneecaps were warming pans. We felt wonderfully cozy, especially since it was so cold outside — and outside the blankets too, since there was no fire in the room. To truly enjoy bodily warmth, some small part of you must be cold, because no quality in this world exists except by contrast. Nothing exists in itself. If you flatter yourself that you've been comfortable all over for a long time, then you can no longer be said to be comfortable at all. But if, like Queequeg and me in that bed, only the tip of your nose or the crown of your head is slightly chilled, then in your general consciousness you feel most delightfully and unmistakably warm. For this reason, a bedroom should never have a fire — that's one of the luxurious discomforts of the rich. The height of this kind of bliss is having nothing but the blanket between your warmth and the cold outside air. Then you lie like the one warm spark in the heart of an arctic crystal.

We had been sitting hunched like this for some time when all at once I decided to open my eyes. When I'm between sheets, day or night, awake or asleep, I tend to keep my eyes shut to concentrate the snugness of being in bed. Because no person can truly feel their own identity unless their eyes are closed — as if darkness were the proper element of our essence, though light suits our clay better. Opening my eyes and leaving my own pleasant, self-created darkness for the imposed, coarse outer gloom of an unlit midnight, I felt a disagreeable jolt. Nor did I object at all when Queequeg hinted that perhaps we had better light a lamp, since we were wide awake and he badly wanted a few quiet puffs from his tomahawk pipe. I should mention that I'd been dead set against his smoking in bed the night before; yet see how elastic our stiff prejudices become once love starts to bend them. Now I liked nothing better than having Queequeg smoke beside me — even in bed — because he seemed so full of serene, domestic contentment. I no longer worried about the landlord's fire insurance. I was alive only to the condensed, confidential comfort of sharing a pipe and a blanket with a real friend. With our shaggy jackets around our shoulders, we passed the tomahawk pipe back and forth until a blue hanging canopy of smoke slowly gathered above us, glowing in the flame of the newly lit lamp.

Whether it was that this undulating canopy of smoke carried the savage away to far-distant scenes, I don't know, but he now spoke of his native island; and, eager to hear his history, I begged him to go on and tell it. He gladly agreed. Though at the time I understood quite a few of his words only poorly, later disclosures, after I had grown more familiar with his broken phrasing, now allow me to present the whole story, such as it may prove to be, in the mere skeleton I give here.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 11 — Natkjole
paragraphs: Vi havde ligget i sengen og snakket og døset af og til, mens Queequeg indimellem kærligt smed sine brune, tatoverede ben over mine og trak dem til sig igen. Vi var så helt og aldeles venlige og frie og uformelle sammen. Til sidst jagede vores lange samtaler den lille smule søvnighed væk, vi havde tilbage, og vi fik lyst til at stå op — selv om der stadig var et stykke til daggry.

Vi blev så vågne, at det blev trættende at ligge ned. Lidt efter lidt satte vi os op med dynerne stoppet godt ind om os og lænede os op ad sengegavlen med vores fire knæ trukket tæt sammen og vores to næser bøjet ind over dem, som om knæskællene var sengevarmere. Vi havde det vidunderligt hyggeligt, især fordi der var så koldt udenfor — også udenfor tæpperne, for der var intet bål i værelset. For virkelig at nyde kropsvarme må en lille del af en være kold, for ingen egenskab i denne verden findes undtagen ved modsætning. Intet findes i sig selv. Hvis du smigrer dig selv med, at du længe har haft det behageligt over det hele, kan man slet ikke længere sige, at du har det behageligt. Men hvis kun spidsen af din næse eller issen af dit hoved er en smule kold, sådan som hos Queequeg og mig i den seng, så føler du i din almene bevidsthed en dejlig og umiskendelig varme. Derfor bør et soveværelse aldrig have ild — det er en af de rige mænds luksuriøse ubehageligheder. Toppen af denne slags salighed er at have kun tæppet mellem din varme og den kolde luft udenfor. Så ligger du som den ene varme gnist i hjertet af en arktisk krystal.

Vi havde siddet sådan sammenkrøbet et godt stykke tid, da jeg pludselig besluttede at åbne øjnene. Når jeg ligger mellem lagnerne, dag eller nat, vågen eller sovende, plejer jeg at holde øjnene lukkede for at samle hyggen ved at ligge i seng. For intet menneske kan virkelig mærke sin egen identitet, med mindre øjnene er lukkede — som om mørket var vores væsens rette element, selv om lyset passer bedre til vores ler. Da jeg åbnede øjnene og forlod mit eget behagelige, selvskabte mørke for den påtvungne, grove ydre dysterhed i en ubelyst midnat, mærkte jeg et ubehageligt ryk. Jeg havde heller ikke noget imod det, da Queequeg antydede, at vi måske hellere kunne tænde en lampe, siden vi var lysvågne, og han havde sådan lyst til et par rolige drag af sin tomahawkpibe. Jeg skal nævne, at jeg aftenen før havde været helt imod, at han røg i sengen; men se, hvor smidige vores stive fordomme bliver, når først kærligheden begynder at bøje dem. Nu var der intet, jeg hellere ville, end at have Queequeg til at ryge ved siden af mig — selv i sengen — for han virkede så fuld af rolig, huslig tilfredshed. Jeg bekymrede mig ikke mere om værtens brandforsikring. Jeg havde kun sans for den tætte, fortrolige hygge i at dele en pibe og et tæppe med en ægte ven. Med vores lodne jakker over skuldrene rakte vi tomahawkpiben frem og tilbage, til en blå, hængende himmel af røg langsomt samlede sig over os og glødede i skæret fra den nytændte lampe.

Om det var, fordi denne bølgende røghimmel førte vilden bort til fjerne steder, ved jeg ikke, men han begyndte nu at tale om sin hjemø; og da jeg var ivrig efter at høre hans historie, bad jeg ham fortsætte og fortælle den. Det ville han gerne. Selv om jeg dengang kun dårligt forstod en hel del af hans ord, gør senere beretninger, efter at jeg var blevet fortrolig med hans brudte måde at tale på, at jeg nu kan give hele historien, sådan som den nu end måtte vise sig at være, i det blotte skelet, som jeg gengiver her.
